docs.title: U.S. History Concept Taxonomy
docs.text: This taxonomy organizes the 450 concepts in the U.S. History learning graph into 12 thematic categories. Each category has a short TaxonomyID used in the CSV and JSON files.

docs.title: 1. Foundation Concepts (FOUND)
docs.text: TaxonomyID: FOUND Color: SteelBlue Foundational constitutional, legal, and governance concepts that underpin U.S. political life across all eras. Includes federalism, constitutional amendments, separation of powers, checks and balances, judicial review, and structural features of American democracy. Also includes economic and social foundations that span multiple periods (immigration history, labor rights, income inequality, etc.).

docs.title: 2. Period 1 – New World and Early Contact (NEWWLD)
docs.text: TaxonomyID: NEWWLD Color: DarkGoldenrod Concepts from c. 1491–1607 covering pre-Columbian civilizations, European exploration, the Columbian Exchange, Spanish/French/Dutch contact, encomienda system, and early consequences of contact for Indigenous peoples.

docs.title: 3. Period 2 – Colonial America (COLAM)
docs.text: TaxonomyID: COLAM Color: Peru Concepts from 1607–1754: the establishment and development of the thirteen colonies, colonial economies and social structures, slavery and indentured servitude, triangular trade, mercantilism, colonial governance, the Great Awakening, and early regional differences.

docs.title: 4. Period 3 – Revolution and Early Republic (REVOL)
docs.text: TaxonomyID: REVOL Color: DarkGreen Concepts from 1754–1800: the French and Indian War, causes of the American Revolution, the Declaration of Independence, Revolutionary War, Articles of Confederation, Constitutional Convention, Bill of Rights, and the Washington and Adams administrations.

docs.title: 5. Period 4 – Expansion and Reform (EXPAN)
docs.text: TaxonomyID: EXPAN Color: LimeGreen Concepts from 1800–1848: Jeffersonian democracy, westward expansion, the Era of Good Feelings, Jacksonian democracy, Indian Removal, Manifest Destiny, the Mexican-American War, abolitionism, women's rights, the Industrial Revolution in America, and antebellum reform movements.

docs.title: 6. Period 5 – Civil War and Reconstruction (CIVWR)
docs.text: TaxonomyID: CIVWR Color: Crimson Concepts from 1844–1877: sectionalism, the path to civil war, the Civil War itself, Reconstruction amendments, Radical Reconstruction, Freedmen's Bureau, and the failure of Reconstruction leading to the Redeemer South.

docs.title: 7. Period 6 – Gilded Age and Immigration (GILDD)
docs.text: TaxonomyID: GILDD Color: Gold Concepts from 1865–1898: industrialization, railroad expansion, robber barons, labor movements, new immigration, urbanization, political machines, the Populist movement, Native American conflicts, and Gilded Age politics.

docs.title: 8. Period 7 – Progressivism and WWI (PROGR)
docs.text: TaxonomyID: PROGR Color: Teal Concepts from 1890–1920: the Progressive Era, muckrakers, Theodore Roosevelt and Woodrow Wilson, trust-busting, women's suffrage, the NAACP, U.S. imperialism, the Spanish-American War, and U.S. involvement in World War I through the Treaty of Versailles.

docs.title: 9. Period 8 – 1920s and Great Depression (DEPRS)
docs.text: TaxonomyID: DEPRS Color: DarkSlateBlue Concepts from 1920–1941: consumer culture, the Harlem Renaissance, Prohibition, nativism, the 1929 crash, the Great Depression, Hoover's response, the New Deal, the Dust Bowl, and the rise of fascism abroad.

docs.title: 10. Period 9 – WWII and Early Cold War (WWII)

Welcome to This Chapter!

Let's investigate the evidence! In this chapter we'll explore one of the most consequential periods in American history. Get ready to think critically, question assumptions, and draw your own conclusions.

Key Insight

Liberty's Tip

This is the tip style — used for hints and helpful guidance. Always check the source date, author, and audience before accepting a historical claim at face value.

docs.title: Warning
docs.text:
Common Mistake

This is the warning style — used to alert students to common misconceptions or logical errors. Watch out for hindsight bias: just because an outcome seems obvious now doesn't mean it was predictable then.

docs.title: Encourage

You Can Do This!

This is the encouraging style — used for difficult or dense content. Primary source analysis can feel challenging at first. That's completely normal. With practice you'll start reading historical documents like a detective.

Great Work!

This is the celebration style — used at the end of major sections. You've just worked through one of the most complex chapters in this course. That takes real intellectual effort — well done!

MAP CONTENT — label and shade each of the following culture regions with distinct, harmonious colors: NORTHEAST: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy (Great Lakes / upstate New York), Algonquian peoples (Atlantic seaboard) SOUTHEAST: Mississippian culture centered on Cahokia (near modern St. Louis), Cherokee homeland (Appalachians), Choctaw / Chickasaw / Creek territories GREAT PLAINS: Lakota / Sioux, Comanche, Cheyenne, and Arapaho ranges; mark bison migration corridors with subtle dotted arrows SOUTHWEST: Ancestral Pueblo / Anasazi (Four Corners region), Hohokam (Sonoran Desert, Arizona), Mogollon, Navajo / Diné, Apache GREAT BASIN: Paiute, Shoshone, Ute territories NORTHWEST COAST: Chinook, Tlingit, Haida, Salish — mark coastal trade canoe routes with thin blue lines PLATEAU: Nez Perce, Yakama CALIFORNIA: Chumash, Ohlone, Yurok — note dense population concentration ARCTIC / SUBARCTIC: Inuit (Thule culture) along northern coastline, Athabascan interior MESOAMERICAN BORDER: indicate Aztec / Mexica empire to the south in muted tones (just northern tip visible) KEY SITES TO MARK WITH ICONS: - Cahokia Mounds (largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, ~20,000 pop.) - Chaco Canyon (Ancestral Pueblo ceremonial center) - Poverty Point, Louisiana (ancient mound complex) - Mesa Verde cliff dwellings - Serpent Mound, Ohio TRADE NETWORKS: overlay thin dashed lines showing the major inter-regional trade routes connecting these cultures (shell trade from Gulf Coast, obsidian from Rockies, copper from Great Lakes) CARTOGRAPHIC STYLE: - Parchment or aged cream background with subtle texture - Soft watercolor-style shading for regional territories with semi-transparent fills - Clean, readable serif labels in dark brown or black ink - Decorative compass rose (bottom right), scale bar (bottom left) - Small inset illustrations: a longhouse (Northeast), pueblo cliff dwelling (Southwest), totem pole (Northwest), earthen mound (Southeast) - Bold title "Major Indigenous Civilizations Before 1492" at the top center in a serif display font - Subtitle in smaller type: "North America — Approximate Cultural Regions" - Soft drop shadows on labels for legibility - Professional legend box (lower left) with color key for culture regions OVERALL FEEL: authoritative, respectful, richly detailed — suitable for an Advanced Placement or college-level US History textbook. Color palette: muted earth tones (terracotta, sage green, ochre, slate blue, warm brown) with white text labels outlined for contrast against the terrain base. Aspect ratio 16:9, 4K resolution, photorealistic cartographic illustration style.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).

docs.title: Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text: This interactive viewer allows you to explore the learning graph for this course.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Search: Type in the search box to find specific concepts
  • Category Filtering: Use checkboxes to show/hide concept categories
  • Interactive Navigation: Click and drag to explore, scroll to zoom
  • Statistics: View real-time counts of visible nodes and edges

docs.title: Using the Viewer
docs.text:
1. Search for Concepts: Start typing in the search box to find concepts. Click on a result to focus on that node.

  2. Filter by Category: Use the category checkboxes in the sidebar to show or hide groups of related concepts. Use "Check All" or "Uncheck All" for bulk operations.

  3. Navigate the Graph:

  4. Drag to pan around the graph
  5. Scroll to zoom in and out

  6. Click on a node to select it and highlight its connections

  7. View Statistics: The sidebar shows counts of visible nodes, edges, and foundational concepts.

docs.title: Graph Structure
docs.text:
• Foundational Concepts (left side): Prerequisites with no dependencies
  • Advanced Concepts (right side): Topics that build on multiple prerequisites
  • Edges: Arrows point from a concept to its prerequisites
